books: Tsai I-ling (Chinese: 蔡依翎; born September 15, 1980), known professionally as Jolin Tsai or simply Jolin (Chinese: 蔡依林), is a Taiwanese singer, songwriter, record producer, and actress. Referred to as the "Queen of C-Pop", she is one of the most influential figures in Chinese-language popular culture. Known for her continual reinvention of musical styles, visual presentation, and performance, Tsai has played a significant role in the development of contemporary Mandopop, particularly through her popularization of dance-pop in the Chinese-speaking world. She exercises substantial creative control over her career, and her work has frequently explored themes of identity, gender, sexuality, self-expression, and contemporary social issues, while achieving both commercial success and critical acclaim.

Born in Hsinchuang, Taiwan, Tsai rose to prominence in 1998 after winning a singing competition organized by MTV Mandarin. She made her recording debut with 1019 in 1999, establishing herself as a leading teen idol. With Magic (2003), she underwent a significant artistic transition toward dance-pop, a direction she further developed with Dancing Diva (2006). The latter earned her first Golden Melody Award and established her as a prominent figure in Chinese-language dance-pop. She subsequently received widespread critical and award recognition for albums including Muse (2012), Play (2014), Ugly Beauty (2018), and Pleasure (2025). With nine Golden Melody Awards, she is the most awarded female Mandopop artist in the history of the awards.

With more than 25 million records sold, Tsai is the highest-selling Taiwanese female recording artist since 2000. Since the release of Magic in 2003, each of her studio albums has been the best-selling album by a female artist in Taiwan in its respective year of release, with four also becoming the country's best-selling album overall.

Faye Wong (Chinese: 王菲; pinyin: Wáng Fēi; born 8 August 1969) is a Hong Kong singer-songwriter and actress. Early in her career, she briefly used the stage name Shirley Wong (王靖雯). Born in Beijing, she moved to Hong Kong at the age of 18. Her debut album Shirley Wong (1989) was in Cantonese and her breakthrough came with the Cantopop song "Fragile Woman" in 1992. She established her style by blending alternative music with Chinese pop, and since the late 1990s has recorded primarily in her native Mandarin. In 2000, Wong was recognised by Guinness World Records as the best selling Cantopop female artist, having sold an estimated 9.7 million copies of her albums by March 2000. Upon her second marriage in 2005, she withdrew from the limelight and moved back to Beijing, making only occasional stage appearances.

In 2009, Wong was voted the second most influential Chinese celebrity of the past 60 years in a poll conducted by the State Council Information Office to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the People's Republic of China.
One of the biggest names in the Chinese-speaking world, Wong has also gained followings in Japan and Southeast Asia. In the West, she is perhaps best known for starring in Wong Kar-wai's films Chungking Express (1994) and 2046 (2004). Often titled "diva" or "heavenly queen" in Chinese, Wong has gained a reputation for her "cool" personality. In Encyclopedia of Contemporary Chinese Culture, Jeroen de Kloet characterised her as "singer, actress, mother, celebrity, royalty, sex symbol and diva all at the same time."

Zhou Xiaohong (traditional Chinese: 周小紅; simplified Chinese: 周小红; pinyin: Zhōu Xiǎohóng; Wade–Giles: Chou1 Hsiao3hung2; born Su Pu; August 1, 1920 – September 22, 1957), known professionally as Zhou Xuan (Chinese: 周璇; pinyin: Zhōu Xuán), also romanized as Chow Hsuan (Wade–Giles: Chou1 Hsüan2), was a Chinese singer and film actress. By the 1940s, she had become one of China's
Seven Great Singing Stars. Nicknamed the "Golden Voice" (金嗓子; Jīn sǎng zi), she was the best known of the seven, and had a concurrent movie career until 1954. She recorded more than 200 songs and appeared in over 40 films in her career.

Yoshiko Yamaguchi (Japanese: 山口淑子 Yamaguchi Yoshiko; Chinese: 山口淑子 Shānkǒu Shūzǐ; 12 February 1920 – 7 September 2014) was a Japanese singer, actress, journalist, and politician. Born in China, she had an international career in film in China, Hong Kong, Japan, and the United States.
Early in her career the Manchukuo Film Association concealed her Japanese origin, and she went by the Chinese name Li Hsiang-lan (李香蘭), rendered in Japanese as Ri Kōran. This allowed her to convincingly portray Chinese characters in Japanese propaganda movies. After the war she appeared in Japanese films under her birth name and in several American films under the stage name Shirley Yamaguchi.

Upon marrying her second husband she quit acting and worked as a journalist in the late 1950s under the name Yoshiko Ōtaka (大鷹 淑子, Ōtaka Yoshiko). She was elected as a member of the Japanese parliament in 1974 and served for 18 years. After retiring from politics she served as vice president of the Asian Women's Fund.
